content: Chagas disease, also known as American trypanosomiasis, is an infectious disease caused by the protozoan parasite Trypanosoma cruzi. Globally, it is estimated that 5 to 8 million people are infected, with an incidence rate of approximately 100 to 400 cases per 100,000 individuals. The disease is most prevalent in South America, where it is considered the most common parasitic infection. Other modes of transmission include blood transfusion, organ transplantation, oral ingestion, breastfeeding, and vertical transmission from mother to child. After transmission, the incubation period for T. cruzi is typically 1 to 2 weeks. During the acute phase of infection, 90% to 95% of individuals remain asymptomatic. However, the parasite persists in the body, and clinical manifestations often appear years or even decades later. Approximately one-third of infected individuals develop chronic Chagas disease, which is characterized by cardiac conduction system dysfunction, gastrointestinal denervation leading to esophageal or colonic dysfunction (megaesophagus and megacolon), or both. Acute Chagas disease is usually diagnosed through a peripheral blood smear, where the T. cruzi parasite can be visually identified. Chronic Chagas disease, on the other hand, is more challenging to diagnose and often requires serological testing or polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assays. Benznidazole and nifurtimox are the only antimicrobial therapies with proven efficacy against T. cruzi infection. Although neither drug is FDA-approved, they can be obtained under investigational protocols. These medications are used to treat congenital infections, acute infections, and chronic infections in younger patients (typically under 50 to 55 years of age) or those with early cardiomyopathy. Chronic Chagas disease frequently leads to congestive heart failure. Patients with Chagas cardiomyopathy often present with right bundle branch block (RBBB) or other arrhythmias. The heart becomes dilated and hypertrophied, with areas of fibrosis, particularly at the apex, and mural thrombi are often present. Histologically, the myocardium shows infiltration by lymphocytes and macrophages, interstitial edema, and fibrosis, with the inflammatory reaction being most severe around the right bundle branch. In addition to cardiac complications, patients may develop megaesophagus or megacolon due to gastrointestinal denervation. The parasite T. cruzi was first identified in pre-Columbian times in South America. Carlos Chagas, a Brazilian bacteriologist, discovered the association between the triatomine insect and T. cruzi. He named the pathogen in honor of his mentor, Oswaldo Cruz. Benznidazole, the first antimicrobial agent effective against T. cruzi, was introduced in 1966. The pathophysiology of Chagas disease is rooted in inflammation. During the acute phase, parasitemia occurs, characterized by parasitic replication and host immune responses. This leads to clinical manifestations. In the chronic phase, persistent low-grade inflammation is thought to contribute to multisystem involvement. The exact mechanisms of chronic disease are not fully understood but may involve either residual parasites that evade immune clearance or autoimmune processes. Gross pathology of acute Chagas disease reveals inflammation, while chronic disease is marked by tissue dilation, congestion, fibrosis, and wall thickening. Microscopically, acute disease shows mononuclear and lymphocytic infiltration, which can lead to tissue denervation and fibrous scar formation over time. Chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy (CCM) is histologically characterized by diffuse and patchy chronic myocarditis, interstitial mononuclear cell infiltrates, and destruction of myocardial fibers with fibrotic replacement. Autopsy studies of patients with end-stage Chagas disease often reveal grossly enlarged hearts and left ventricular apical aneurysms. Chagas disease must be differentiated from other conditions that cause cardiomyopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, or gastrointestinal dysfunction, such as electrophysiological cardiac diseases, gastrointestinal hypomotility disorders, and malignancies. The disease is most commonly reported in South America, but cases have also been identified in Central America and among South American immigrants in non-endemic regions. Individuals of all age groups can acquire Chagas disease, including neonates through vertical transmission. Elderly patients are more likely to exhibit chronic manifestations. While there is no racial predilection, the majority of cases occur in individuals of Hispanic origin due to the endemicity of the disease in South America. Risk factors for Chagas disease include living in endemic regions, particularly in homes constructed with mud, sticks, or straw, as these structures are conducive to triatomine infestation. Other risk factors include consuming contaminated food or water and receiving blood transfusions or organ transplants from infected donors. Neonates are at higher risk if born to seropositive mothers or if breastfeeding from mothers with cracked or bleeding nipples. The natural history of Chagas disease begins with an acute phase, during which most individuals are asymptomatic. When symptoms do occur, they are often nonspecific, such as fever, myalgia, fatigue, and anorexia. Severe cases may present with myocarditis or meningoencephalitis. Chronic symptoms are typically related to cardiac or gastrointestinal complications. Chagas cardiomyopathy is the most common chronic manifestation, accounting for 80% to 90% of cases. Patients with Chagas cardiomyopathy often die within two years of symptom onset. On physical examination, Chagas disease may present with fever, tachycardia, cardiac rhythm abnormalities, hepatosplenomegaly, and lymphadenopathy. A classic sign of acute Chagas disease is Romaña's sign, which is characterized by unilateral eyelid swelling at the site of parasite entry. Other physical findings are usually related to cardiac or gastrointestinal complications. Laboratory diagnosis of acute Chagas disease relies on the detection of T. cruzi in a peripheral blood smear. In chronic cases, serological testing is often required, with positivity for both whole parasite lysate and recombinant antigen assays being necessary for diagnosis. PCR is sensitive in acute cases, such as those following organ transplantation, but its sensitivity and specificity are variable in chronic disease and depend on the pre-test probability. Electrocardiographic findings in Chagas cardiomyopathy commonly include right bundle branch block (RBBB) and atrioventricular (AV) block. Treatment of Chagas disease involves the use of benznidazole or nifurtimox. These drugs are effective against T. cruzi infection but are not FDA-approved and must be obtained through investigational protocols. They are used to treat congenital, acute, and chronic infections in younger patients or those with early cardiomyopathy. Primary prevention strategies include the use of insecticides to control triatomine vectors, improving housing construction materials to reduce vector habitats, and screening blood and organ donors in endemic regions. Although investigational therapies for chronic Chagas disease are being studied, no new pharmacologic treatments have proven to be more effective than the current standard of care with benznidazole or nifurtimox.
